utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-01-47-PT, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic, Mehmed Alagic, and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May I have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, good afternoon counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mr. Michael Johnson, Chief of Prosecutions, Madam Jocelyne Bodson, senior trial attorney, Ms. Cynthia Fairweather, legal officer, Ms. Diana Dicklich, and myself, trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Edina Residovic, an attorney from Sarajevo, and I'm here defending General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, attorney from Sarajevo, and together with Mr. Johnson Jones, I will defend Mr. Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm attorney Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and together with Mr. Dixon, we will be representing Mr. Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would like to find out from the accused persons whether they can follow the proceedings in a language they understand. Do you understand the proceedings? THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do understand entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one, please. THE ACCUSED ALAGIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Madam Judge, I do understand the language that I can hear in my headphones and the language I can see on the display. THE ACCUSED KUBURA: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can understand everything. I can hear and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is a Status Conference under 65 bis. This is a Status Conference under Rule 65 bis. I'm aware that the parties had a meeting with the Senior Legal Officer and the other legal counsel for Chambers, and that several matters were discussed, and the Trial Chamber has been briefed. So this Status Conference is scheduled to hear other matters that may be of concern to the parties, not a review of the meeting that was held, and also to hear whether there are any concerns in the welfare of the accused persons. So I'll start with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, since all of the interesting matters were discussed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, since all the interesting matters were discussed on the Tuesday meeting, from the Prosecution there's at this stage nothing to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If I may ask the Prosecution regarding protective measures on the materials that have been served on the Defence and that are going to be served on the Defence. I was wondering whether there are any concerns that they may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, so far, the supporting material was filed confidentially, and the material cannot be disclosed to the public. Otherwise, we will file a motion requesting protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Does that mean that there is any -- there are any protective measures that the Defence may not know about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. I wanted to find out from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you have said on the 27th, we looked into 11 issues which are of interest to the parties and the proceedings, and for preparations for the trial, and you have been informed about this. I would just like to add that certain obligations undertaken at that meeting have already been met by the Prosecutor. Yesterday, we were given part of the annexes which we had told them would be of interest to the Defence. I also wish to add that after the meeting, I received your supplemental order concerning the preparation of our motions, and regarding that, I would like to give you my opinion. In your order, it is quite clear that the party wishing to reply to the reply of the other party, based on the motion, needs to ask for leave to do so within three days, based on Article 21(1) of the Statute, which provides that all of the parties are equal before this Tribunal. I would like to suggest the following to you: Each party which submits a request will offer its arguments in favour of this request, so that the other party can familiarise itself with the arguments and the other party can reply to these arguments. Very frequently, and I know this based on my experience in working before this Tribunal, there are supplemental arguments given by the opposing party, and we believe that it would be fair to provide an opportunity to the other party to reply to this. So with respect to your order, I would like to suggest the following: Should the Court decide to make a public hearing to allow the parties to state their arguments, then I would agree with your order; but however, should the Court decide to give its opinion based on the written submissions, then I would like to ask you to reconsider your order and to allow the other party to bring out its arguments, because in giving its reply, this party is actually becoming familiar with the arguments of the other side for the first time. I was not aware of this order of yours prior to the meeting we had on the 27th, so this is why I brought this issue up. And one more thing. We have some joint submissions and some individual submissions. To this date, we still do not know, albeit we asked to be granted a public hearing as far as the form of the indictment is concerned, but so far we do not know whether the Chamber has decided to grant us such a hearing or not. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If I may answer the last point on the request for a hearing on the form of indictment. In practice, the Trial Chambers do not grant oral hearings, for the simple reason that the parties are expected to set out their submissions, the basis for their submissions, and whatever else they want to say in their written motion. This is to avoid having too hearings, because we are quite crowded in terms of courtrooms. So it is the practice that you have to make your submissions in full, so that the other parties are fully informed of the basis of your motion, and then they can respond also in writing. So it is not our practice to have oral hearings, because we always feel that oral hearings, in practice, have always been a repetition of what has been put in writing. So if it's a question of expanding on them, please, the parties must expand on these written motions as much as possible so that nothing is left out, and then the other parties can also respond fully, and then the Trial Chamber can have all the materials they need to decide on the motion. As for the motion on the form of indictment, it is not the intention of the Trial Chamber to have an oral hearing. However, if for any reason any party feels that what they've already submitted may not be sufficient, they should, of course, put in supplementary submissions. We have no intention of holding an oral hearing for this particular motion. The other point you raised about having a short time having to respond, perhaps in three days, that the Trial Chamber will consider. But like I said, from now on the parties must bear in mind that any written motion must be fully defended, fully explored, so that the other party doesn't have a problem responding fully and the Trial Chamber will have all the materials they need to work on their decision, to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I would like to be sure that I have understood your reply. Does that mean that we are automatically given leave to reply, or do we need to ask for your leave to reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which one? Regarding which one?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On any submission, not just our side but any side that is replying to a motion that was submitted. Usually, supplemental arguments are given. Now, does the side that has put in the motion in the first place, does that side have a right to give additional arguments to the reply, or does that side need to ask for leave within three days to give such additional reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we will stick to our routine. The party who wishes to respond will still have to apply for leave. I was discussing the other -- generally, on the motion, when you file any motion. I was trying to say parties should bear in mind that every matter that has to be considered must be put in the written motion, because it is not the practice of the Trial Chamber or, indeed, the Tribunal, to have oral hearings on motions. We try to avoid that as much as possible. So for the order where you already have to apply for leave within three days, that still stands. Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at our yesterday's meeting with your legal officer, we discussed all of the contentious issues. It was especially important for us to have an order issued for an urgent medical examination for General Alagic. We received such order this morning and we would like to thank you for such prompt reaction. As far as the confidential material is concerned, which is something you asked the Prosecution about, we would like to receive the order of Judge Riad, dated 13th July 2001, in which, when confirming the indictment against Hadzihasanovic, Alagic and Kubura, it was also ordered not to publicly disclose supporting material for the indictment. It is our interest to receive a copy of that order, because otherwise Defence will be put in an especially difficult position and it will face a dilemma whether this material, which perhaps also entails confidential material, could be given further to the investigators or not, because the Defence perhaps could violate one of the Tribunal's orders and be held in contempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. If I may answer that one right away. The Trial Chamber did consider this, and we are of the view that if there are any such orders that may not be known by the Defence, the Trial Chamber is going to issue an order lifting protective measures, I think by Wednesday, 5th of December, unless the Prosecution files a motion expressing their concerns or whatever protective measures they would like still to persist on the documents already disclosed or yet to be disclosed. So the Trial Chamber is ready to lift them if -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: First of all, there is no confidential material in the supporting materials. That's basically a non-issue. Secondly, the Prosecution would have no objections against such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence for the third accused fully supports the statements of Defence for General Hadzihasanovic and General Alagic, so we have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I take it there are no concerns regarding the status of the accused in the Detention Unit, apart from the motions for provisional release which are still pending. I take it that there is nothing, so I would like to discuss two matters, especially with the Prosecution, which concern Trial Chambers in the -- once the trial starts. And this is the way you handle the Prosecution witnesses. We do have a few problems once the trial starts, and we do notice sometimes that there are witnesses who would very well be well cutted for -- under Rule 92 bis, if the Prosecution were minded to do so. And the reason we have this rule is to try, as much as possible, to cut down on trial time. The Prosecution can have these statements of their witnesses. Of course, it will be open to the Defence to apply that those witnesses be cross-examined if they have any issues with the contents of the statements, and even if those witnesses come for cross-examination only, at least the time will be spared for other matters, for other witnesses who have to be heard orally. So I would like to impress upon the Prosecution as much as possible to use this Rule, within the confines of the Rules -- of the practices where it applies. And the other point which creates problems during a trial are documents, exhibits. We do have problems with translation, because of the overload, obviously, but there is a lot of room for improvement in that area on the documents that the Prosecution wish to use during the trial process. Sometimes we have documents which are only photocopies, and sometimes no satisfactory reasons are given why the originals are not available. Sometimes the photocopies are not legible to anyone, and there are cases where even the Prosecution sometimes have not been able to tell the Trial Chamber satisfactorily what the document is all about. These are very important matters, and they do delay proceedings most of the time. On translation, as much as possible, the full translation should be obtained before any document can be used as an exhibit. Trial Chambers are not satisfied with what is called draft translations. The other problem with documents we experience during the trials is that sometimes the Prosecution will hand over a bunch of documents to the Defence without describing each of those documents in the bundle, and when the trial starts, the Defence will say that they were never given -- such a document was never disclosed, simply because it was among a bunch of documents not properly described to the Defence. That should be avoided. These points relate also to the Defence. It's also important for them to handle their documents properly, to avoid delays, to avoid adjournments once the trial starts. And I also want to explain to the Defence the processes under Rule 92 bis. It does not mean that if a statement of a witness is submitted by the Prosecution, then the Defence are accepting all the contents of that statement. All it means is that instead of having the witness come into the courtroom to give evidence orally, we are serving on time, we have the written statement there, and the Defence are free to ask that that witness be cross-examined fully on all the points that are in the statement. I think I will also discuss the possible trial dates in the view of the Trial Chamber. Of course, the Trial Chamber has been informed by the Senior Legal Officer about the concerns of the Prosecution, and also the concerns of the Defence. But as both parties are aware, the Tribunal is trying very hard to get these cases going, because of the other cases that are coming up, and more and more may get arrested and others may surrender to the Tribunal. So we would very much like to move on with the backload of trials. This is why we have got ad litem Judges. At any time a Trial Chamber may be constituted to go ahead and try any cases that may be ready. And looking at the work that the parties are doing so far and what is yet to be done, the Trial Chamber is of the view that it is possible for this trial to commence in the month of April, 2002, and the Trial Chamber would like to move the parties to work towards that month as any of the dates that after the Easter holidays. The Trial Chamber is likely to issue a Scheduling Order for the trial to commence then. Of course, that means working at full speed, dealing with the preparations that may come under the Rules, and also it means for the Defence also to work at full speed and get on with the preparations for the defence so that we comply with the pre-trial rules and complete the pre-trial procedures as early as possible next year. The Trial Chamber does not see any other matters that may hinder the progress of the pre-trial stage and the possibility of having the trial start in the month of April next year. I hope that is understood, and I do hope that the parties will come up during their meetings with the Senior Legal Officer, with whatever problems they may have. In the meantime, the Trial Chamber will deal with the motions that are pending, hopefully to have the decisions made before the recess this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a Defence objection to commencing in April next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll turn to my learned friend Ms. Residovic in a moment to address you on that. But as Your Honour mentioned, there were extensive discussions on this subject with your Senior Legal Officer at a Pre-Status Conference three days ago at which we detailed at great length the tremendous difficulties with documents that the Defence need to thoroughly examine in order to fully benefit from the right which the accused enjoys to have adequate facilities and time to prepare their defence. And moreover, there is, of course, the right to a fair trial which the accused enjoy. I would submit that you can have a trial until April or you can have a fair trial, but you can't have both in April. It's simply too soon and it's a matter of some dismay to hear you announce that, given at the end of the discussions we had on Tuesday it was agreed by the Senior Legal Officer and by the Prosecution that it would be inappropriate at this moment to set a trial date. That was given the fact that preliminary motions have not even yet been fully disposed of. Disclosure, pursuant to Rule 66(A)(2) only began two days ago and it's not envisaged that that will be completed until the end of January next year. Until we have full disclosure and the preliminary motions fully disposed of so that the accused know the indictment they will actually be facing at trial, it's unrealistic to posit a date so early next year. So I would request Your Honour to reconsider, and the Chamber to reconsider, that indication of a trial date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the interests of a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is very much aware of the rights of the accused and is very much aware of the stages that the pre-trial stage has to go through, and is also fully briefed about the documentation that the Defence have to go through, but the Trial Chamber is of the view that given all the time that we have from now on up to the end of, say, February, the documentation should have been completed by then, and also the fact that -- the Prosecution appear to have made an indication as to when all the documents from their archives, which are under discussion between the parties, are likely to be taken back to the archives. So the Trial Chamber is of the view that that will give the Defence ample time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may address you as to that. I think it would be useful to have an indication from the Prosecution of how long it took them to review those archives. From what I understood from our meeting on Tuesday, it took a team of the Prosecution many months to review those documents, and I would ask the Prosecution to address us as he did on Tuesday, as to the numbers of documents, the tens of thousands of documents in those archives which are relevant to this case and that should throw light on the difficulties we're facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but what the Prosecution were doing at the time, really they weren't working on the stages of this -- of only this case. They were looking at the documents as a whole, as the Prosecution as a whole, even including their concerns on the other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it would be useful to hear from the Prosecution on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but it may be useful during your meetings maybe, but I don't think that the Trial Chamber, or indeed this Status Conference, is going to set any deadlines for that sort of preparation. Of course, usually the Trial Chamber would always give sufficient time to the parties when there is a good reason to extend the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you allow me to address you regarding this matter as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, because, like I said, this is a Status Conference, not a review of the meeting which you had with counsel -- with the Senior Legal Officer. Very, very briefly, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interests of my client is to schedule the trial without further delay, but his greatest interest is to have a fair trial. This is why I shall confirm the arguments that we brought out during the meeting, as Mr. Jones has described. But based on what the Prosecutor has said, we have to check 30.000 documents that are yet to be returned to the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I would like to ask you to reconsider the fact that we are especially interested in the material from the Blaskic, Kupreskic, and Kordic trials, because in the Blaskic case, at the end of the trial, the Honourable Judge Jorda issued an order to the Prosecution to start investigating those areas where the victims were Croatian soldiers or civilians, which means that that entails some further 10.000 of documents of public nature. And as far as our request to gain access to the confidential documents and testimonies from those cases is concerned, that has not been decided upon yet. So we are hereby asking you and telling you that we took into account all of the arguments, and despite all of our efforts, we were not able to come up with a proposed date for the beginning of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I've taken into account all your submissions and your concerns, and of course the Trial Chamber is also interested in a fair trial. That is non-negotiable. That is well understood. But the Trial Chamber would like to impress upon the parties that it is important that the trial starts most, most likely at least midway next year, at least next year, not later than next year. And of course the Prosecution have understood the concerns. They know what is going on and I'm sure that they will oblige and they will take their concerns -- the concerns of the Defence very seriously. So I don't think that the Defence, indeed, the accused, should be unduly worried about whether or not their trial will be compromised as far as fairness is concerned. That will never happen, not here in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution, any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution only wants to raise one issue. Out of the hundred witnesses we are currently envisaging, there are around 65 crime-based witnesses, and the Prosecution invites the Defence again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I hear 65 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Crime-based witnesses. The Prosecution wants to use this opportunity to repeatedly invite the Defence to enter into stipulations and to think about the opportunities that are provided by Rule 94(B).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This reminds me -- I also wanted to find out about expert witnesses. Do you envisage, does the Prosecution envisage having any expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not at the current stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not at the current stage. Yes. Of course, usually in practice what I have observed is that as soon as witness statements are provided or detailed summaries are provided to the Defence, usually it becomes much easier for them to get instructions and be able to stipulate or make admissions on any of the matters that may be raised by the indictment. So it is really up to the Prosecution to move in this direction much faster, and then the Defence can always handle the matter also much more expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: With the supporting materials, we already provided 84 witness statements and we are currently envisaging to rely on only 15, 1-5, witness statements, so the Defence is already aware of almost every single witness statement that could be the basis for stipulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. I'm sure the Defence have understood and they know what their obligations are. In the meantime, the Senior Legal Officer will continue discussing the stages of the preparations between the parties and may also schedule meetings for matters to follow the pre-trial stages much more fully and comply with the deadlines. Unless there are any other matters, otherwise this is the end of the Status Conference and we shall rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
